discovery.title: What can a hearth and post mark reveal about people 13,800 years ago?
discovery.summary: Researchers report a 13,800-year-old Alaska camp with a hearth, a post stain, tools, needles and other remains. They describe the structure as a potential early dwelling, not a definitive house.
discovery.why_it_matters: Evidence of a dwelling can reshape understanding of how early communities organized life and adapted to the far north after reaching the Americas.

discovery.title: Could one new undersea cable move 125 terabytes every second?
discovery.summary: Meta announced Petal, a planned 7,000-kilometer cable linking the U.S. and France. The company says it could carry up to one petabit per second when it comes online in 2029.
discovery.why_it_matters: More transatlantic capacity could change where data-intensive services run and how quickly they reach users, while increasing reliance on ocean-floor infrastructure.

discovery.title: What becomes scarce when internet bandwidth surges?
discovery.summary: A proposed transatlantic undersea cable is designed to carry up to one petabit per second. Its launch is planned for 2029, so the capacity remains a future target rather than a live service.
discovery.why_it_matters: A sharp increase in backbone capacity may shift bottlenecks toward data centers, power supply and network access instead of long-distance transmission alone.

discovery.title: What new species might be hiding in museum drawers?
discovery.summary: A fossil collected about a century ago was identified as Invictibellatrix amberina, a previously unknown megaraptoran dinosaur. Researchers say it is the first megaraptoran identified in Europe.
discovery.why_it_matters: Re-examining old collections can reveal species and evolutionary histories without finding new excavation sites, changing what museums can teach about ancient ecosystems.

discovery.geography: Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean and West Africa
discovery.title: When does a floating seaweed habitat become a coastal burden?
discovery.summary: A recent science broadcast highlights a surge of floating sargassum affecting Atlantic coastlines. Offshore, the algae also provides habitat and food for marine species, making the bloom’s impacts complex.
discovery.why_it_matters: The same drifting algae can support ocean ecosystems offshore and create costly coastal problems when it washes ashore, linking marine ecology, tourism and community response.
